### 3.  Look for an integrating factor \(\mu\) that depends only on \(r^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}\)

Let \(\mu=\mu(r^{2})\).  
Writing \(r^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}\) and using

\]

For points where \(x\neq y\) we can cancel \((x-y)\) and obtain

\[
\frac{\mu'}{\mu}= -\frac{3}{2}\,\frac{1}{r^{2}+1}.
\]

\[
\ln\mu =-\frac{3}{2}\ln(r^{2}+1)+\text{const}
